podcast.title: Early Incarnation and Musical Direction (1993)
podcast.body: By 1993, an early incarnation of The Matthew Good Band existed with different players and string arrangements. This lineup ended that year as Matthew Good felt it wasn't aligning with his desired musical direction. "I mean, back then it was all different players. There were strings involved in it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 1

podcast.title: Total Releases (1995-2009)
podcast.body: By the end of 2009, the band had accumulated 12 releases over a span of 14 years. "At the end of 2009, we have 12 releases over 14 years and a lot of people who have maybe jumped on the train somewhere in the middle didn't realize that you began as part of a folk band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 1

podcast.title: The Edgefest Panda Incident (1999)
podcast.body: During the Matthew Good Band's performance on the main stage at Edgefest in Wilson Park, Barrie, in 1999, Universal Music marketing representative Iber Hamilton, dressed in a giant panda costume, attempted a stage dive during the song "Everything's Automatic." From the 10-12 foot high stage, he launched into the crowd, which unexpectedly parted "like the Red Sea." The panda landed face down on the ground 12 feet below, suffering a bleeding nose (his head was protected by a football helmet within the costume) and was subsequently kicked by some members of the audience. Matthew Good, performing with his microphone back by the monitor lines, did not immediately see what happened but later found Hamilton in the back with a bloody face. This incident later inspired the artwork for the "Loser Anthem" EP. "The crowd parts like the Red Sea. Everybody moves. Panda, bam! Face down on the ground, 12 feet below the stage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 1

podcast.title: Breakup in 2001
podcast.body: The Matthew Good Band dissolved around 2001, an outcome of pervasive internal dysfunction, Matthew's illness, and an unwillingness to tour the `Audio of Being` record. The band members had reached a point where communication broke down, and individuals asserted their indispensability, leading Matthew, who usually tried to "placate" others, to finally end the group. "And that was the end of the Matthew Good Band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 2

podcast.title: Band Name Evolution (Matthew Good Band vs. MGB)
podcast.body: The band initially used the acronym "MGB" on the first 5,000 copies of their debut album, "Last of the Ghetto Astronauts." However, public demand at radio (for "Alabama Motel Room") and retail led people to consistently request "Matthew Good Band." Faced with this popularity, the decision was made to officially adopt Matthew Good's name for the band, partly because early members were not fully committed and often had other academic pursuits. This event, however, was later described as "the beginning of the end" due to escalating ego issues. "The decision was made that that's what we would call it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 1

podcast.title: Dave's Disregard for Band Work
podcast.body: During the writing phase for `Audio of Being` in Whistler, Dave (likely Dave Genn) arrived late because he was busy working with "Hollywood" (presumably Holly McNarland) and in "Ireland." Matthew Good expressed frustration, believing Dave should have prioritized band commitments given their success (a near Triple Platinum album). "Dave came up for a little bit. But unfortunately, he was a little late because he was busy with Hollywood and Ireland working with Hollywood."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 2

podcast.title: Dysfunctional Tour and Matthew's 30th Birthday
podcast.body: The tour supporting `Audio of Being` was marked by extreme dysfunction, with band members refusing to speak to one another. Matthew's 30th birthday occurred on this tour in "Gogory," where he avoided his bandmates by leaving a celebratory cake in his hotel room and going to the Corral Center. He also sustained a back injury in a car accident during the tour. "The whole tour was ridiculous."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 2

podcast.title: Exhaustive Touring Conditions
podcast.body: The band frequently undertook rigorous tours across the country, often playing up to 16 consecutive shows. Traveling in a van, members would sleep with their knees pressed against the seat in front, and showers were taken whenever possible in available band rooms or venues. "I don't know how many times we toured the country in the van, you know, playing 16 shows in a row with your knees pinned up against the seat in front of you."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 1

podcast.title: Featured in "In Their Own Words" Series
podcast.body: Matthew Good Band was featured in the "In Their Own Words" series, a program that brings band members into the studio to share their personal history. "Matthew Good, Finger Leaven..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 1000th Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Internal Dysfunction and Political Dynamics
podcast.body: The Matthew Good Band suffered from significant internal dysfunction, described as "very political and weird," particularly during the creation of `Audio of Being`. This included members vying for publishing rights by injecting ideas and a general lack of communication during tours, ultimately contributing to the band's dissolution. "It might have been even more successful had the Matthew Good band been functioning properly. There was a lot of internal dysfunction."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 2

podcast.title: Post-Name Change Ego Struggles
podcast.body: The formal adoption of "The Matthew Good Band" name led to significant ego issues within the group, which Matthew Good described as "the beginning of the end." To maintain peace and cohesion, he made efforts to placate other members, even going as far as to give up publishing rights and credit that he felt wasn't necessarily due. "From that day forward, ego was about everything."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 1

podcast.title: Publishing Rights Conflicts
podcast.body: During rehearsals for `Audio of Being`, band members deliberately tried to inject their ideas into songs, not purely for creative reasons, but "because they know that if they do, then they can make a case for publishing." This self-serving behavior significantly "hampered" the entire creative and recording process. "People are trying to inject ideas because they know that if they do, then they can make a case for publishing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 2

podcast.title: Top Billing Misperception
podcast.body: The band was publicly perceived as primarily "Matthew Good," giving him top billing despite his personal preference against it. This public misperception was a factor in the band's identity and internal dynamics. "The Matthew Good Band was a group that gave Matt top billing, something that he never wanted. This all came as the result of a public misperception."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 2

podcast.title: Underdogs Album Sales Bet
podcast.body: At Universal or A&M (the specific label was unclear at the time), Paul A. Graham, the head A&R, made an office bet that the "Underdogs" album would not sell more than 30,000 records. Despite this internal skepticism, the album's sales dramatically increased from approximately 20,000 units to over 100,000 within months, largely propelled by the success of the "Operations" music video. "There was an office bed going around where the actual head A&R said that I wouldn't sell more than 30,000 records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Covered by The Matthew Good Band
xref.body: The Matthew Good Band released a cover of a Depeche Mode song on their "Low-Five Besides" EP in 1998. "This is the Matthew Good Band covering DePesh Mode."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 1

xref.title: Gil Norton's Production Work
xref.body: Producer Gil Norton had previously worked on the first few Foo Fighters albums and was committed to producing another Foo Fighters record in 1997, which prevented him from producing The Matthew Good Band's "Underdogs" album. "He had been doing the first few fighters albums by that point. He was just about to do color, didn't he? And that's why he couldn't do it. He couldn't do the record because he was doing the food record, and he'd already committed, but he really wanted to do it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 1

xref.title: Intense Anxiety and Illness During Recording
xref.body: During the recording of the `Audio of Being` album, Matthew Good experienced severe anxiety and was physically ill, throwing up daily for eight months. This period was marked by his sarcoidosis and the worsening internal dysfunction of the Matthew Good Band, making the entire recording process a "nightmare." "Well, I threw up that entire year, every day."

xref.title: Self-Reflection on Band Breakup
xref.body: Matthew Good expressed ongoing guilt and self-doubt regarding the Matthew Good Band's dissolution, questioning whether his undiagnosed illness, his perceived "difficult" personality, or media portrayals of him contributed to the split. He acknowledged these as possibilities and felt it would be ignorant to deny his potential role. "I think I probably look back more and think what the hell was I thinking."
